newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND PUBLISHES SECRET TEXTS FROM EX-PM SPY PROBE.
newsitem.headline: POLAND PUBLISHES SECRET TEXTS FROM EX-PM SPY PROBE.

text.p: Poland's government on Monday published a "White Book" said to contain all documents gathered in a probe of security service allegations that former Prime Minister Jozef Oleksy had collaborated with Moscow spies.

The book, issued to journalists, has more than 450 pages of documents -- many stamped "secret" -- providing a mine of detail but at first sight adding little to widely-leaked outlines of the episode which rocked Poland early this year.
Oleksy, who proclaims his innocence, quit in January after military prosecutors decided to investigate the allegations.
The prosecutors then dropped the probe in April, saying the evidence was clearly inadequate, and Oleksy is now leader of the ex-communists -- dominant party in the ruling coalition.

Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki told a news conference that all materials relating to the case were in the book, except for some names and details kept back to safeguard Polish intelligence and some filthy language cited in transcripts.
Where cuts have been made, they are marked and explained, while even the fruitiest obscenities used by Polish officers can be guessed, as first letters of such words are provided.
The so-called Oleksy affair erupted in December, as Lech Walesa was about to hand over Poland's presidency to ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski, who had won elections.
The outgoing interior minister Andrzej Milczanowski, a Walesa ally, outlined the allegations to a stunned parliament.

But official reports later suggested that the evidence against Oleksy, partly from an alleged mole in Russian intelligence, contained major flaws and gaps -- a message the government hopes will be driven home by the published texts.
Oleksy and his supporters have charged that the accusations were cooked up by pro-Walesa officers for political reasons -- which Milczanowski denies.
"I consider my actions were justified, correct and accurate," the ex-minister told PAP news agency.

The "White Book", due to go on public sale on Tuesday, contains a critical internal report in May by the security service (UOP) about the whole operation, which suggests political motives played a part in the gathering of evidence.

At Monday's news conference, Interior Minister Zbigniew Siemiatkowski said that while Oleksy was clearly not the alleged Moscow spy, codenamed "Olin", in Poland's ruling circles, a hunt was still on to uncover any such agent.
The allegations against Oleksy centred on his contacts with Russian diplomat and intelligence officer Vladimir Alganov.
One theory was that Russian agents may have stirred up the rumpus to make Poland seem chaotic or riddled with spies and harm its bid to enter NATO, which Russia saw as a threat.
The UOP report in the White Book also raises this idea.
"Realisation of operational activities suggests that the threat of a provocation or inspiration from the Russian side was not adequately taken into account," it said.
Views of the affair continue to be shaped by politics.

A parliamentary committee due to report on UOP's role has split on party lines, with members of the ruling coalition calling for Milczanowski to be tried by a State Tribunal while opposition members said any shortcomings in the probe were not serious enough to merit such proceedings.
